parts.quote: Email your receipt by 5 pm today to claim the prize.
You are required to disclose financial documentation in a timely manner or you will be deemed to be disqualified from this prize offer.

rules.quote: Choose simple words, not complicated expressions
rules.specification: The table supplies candidate substitutions, not context-free replacements. Check that the simpler alternative preserves the intended meaning. The everyday-word instructions elsewhere on the page express the same word-choice preference.
rules.violation_condition: A needlessly complicated or formal word or expression is used where a simpler, familiar alternative would preserve the intended meaning.
when: Apply the table's verb-specific recommendations only to the indicated verb uses.
The recommendation against ‘table’ as a verb excludes tabling a document in parliament.
Technical or specialist terms may be used when research shows that the audience uses them; plain language remains the default.
rules.why: G-4 consolidates the repeated plain-word preference; G-2 retains the table's contextual qualifications rather than creating a rule for every substitution.

covers.quote: Clarify expressions people might be unfamiliar with.
Avoid jargon
Remove jargon, slang and idioms.
You can include technical or specialist terms if your research shows your audience uses them.
explain terms – for example, use a glossary

parts.quote: They changed their decision in response to new information.

examples.note: The manual identifies ‘in light of’ as an idiom.

parts.quote: They changed their decision in light of new information.

rules.quote: Avoid (or explain) unusual words, phrases, idioms and so on.
rules.specification: Assess unfamiliarity against the intended audience. Explanations may be supplied in the text or a glossary. This combines the page's removal instruction with its explicit alternative of explaining unusual expressions.
rules.violation_condition: Jargon, slang, idioms or unfamiliar expressions are retained without an explanation that makes their meaning accessible to the intended audience.
when: Avoiding the expression or explaining it satisfies the unusual-expression requirement.
Technical or specialist terms may be retained when research shows that the audience uses them.
Explain specialist terms that readers still need help understanding, including unavoidable terms with special meanings.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3 keep avoidance, explanation and the audience-research permission together; G-4 absorbs the repeated jargon and clarification instructions.

rules.violation_condition: A sentence uses a double negative.
rules.why: This is an independent, text-checkable prohibition, not a restatement of the word-choice rules.

rules.quote: Level AAA requires a lower secondary education reading level, after removal of proper names and titles, (year 7 or between 12 and 14 years old)
rules.specification: The page supplies the target reading level but no assessment method. Do not invent a readability formula or infer that all content is required to achieve Level AAA.
rules.violation_condition: Content intended to satisfy the cited WCAG Level AAA reading-level requirement exceeds lower-secondary reading difficulty after proper names and titles are excluded.
when: Apply only when assessing conformance with the cited WCAG Level AAA reading-level requirement.
Exclude proper names and titles from the reading-level assessment.
rules.why: G-2 keeps the Level AAA condition and exclusions within one reading-level check; this does not create an unconditional AAA requirement.

covers.quote: Use ‘we’, ‘you’ and ‘us’ if you can

parts.quote: We will assess your application within 30 days.

examples.note: The manual presents this as ‘Not this’ for the direct, personal treatment.

rules.quote: Use personal pronouns (like ‘we’, ‘you’, ‘us’) when it suits the voice and tone.
rules.specification: Suitability depends on the intended voice and tone, which this page does not define. Do not require a pronoun in every sentence or turn the accompanying discussion of active voice into a separate prohibition.
rules.violation_condition: Impersonal wording omits personal pronouns where they would suit the content's intended voice and tone.
when: Apply when personal pronouns suit the intended voice and tone.
rules.why: G-4 selects the more precise body instruction and absorbs the heading; G-2 preserves its voice-and-tone condition.

covers.quote: Use inclusive language

rules.quote: Choose words that respect all people, including their rights and their heritage.
rules.specification: Assess respectful treatment in context. The instruction does not require every reference to people to mention their rights or heritage.
rules.violation_condition: Wording refers to people in a way that disrespects them, their rights or their heritage.
rules.why: G-4 uses the actionable body sentence rather than making the broad heading a second rule.

covers.quote: Be selective about shortened forms, such as abbreviations, contractions, acronyms and initialisms.
Some shortened forms are better-known than the full form of the term, for example ‘DNA’.
Try to avoid them altogether if they are used only once or twice.
In content with many specialist terms, reserve shortened forms for the most frequently used terms only.
Spell out other terms in full.

rules.quote: Shorten only the words and phrases that are well known or used many times in your content.
rules.specification: The page explicitly discourages forms used once or twice, but does not quantify ‘many times’, ‘many specialist terms’ or ‘most frequently used’. Preserve those unresolved thresholds rather than inventing counts. The passage lists contractions among shortened forms, although its worked example concerns an organisation initialism.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened form is neither well known nor used many times, is used only once or twice despite the advice to avoid such forms, or abbreviates a less-frequent specialist term in content with many specialist terms.
when: General eligibility is that the word or phrase is well known or used many times in the content.
Avoid shortened forms used only once or twice.
In content with many specialist terms, reserve shortened forms for the most frequently used terms and write other terms in full.
Some shortened forms, such as ‘DNA’, are better known than their full forms.
rules.why: G-2 consolidates the general frequency condition and the stricter specialist-content case; G-4 absorbs the selectivity restatements.

covers.quote: Expand all acronyms on their first use.

examples.note: The full organisation name precedes its initialism.

parts.quote: The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) helps government agencies create digital services.

rules.quote: Spell them out the first time you use them.
rules.specification: The check is clear for acronyms and initialisms. The surrounding passage also lists abbreviations and contractions as shortened forms, but does not explain how first-use expansion applies to ordinary contractions; that wider scope needs review. The page does not explicitly exempt familiar forms from first-use expansion.
rules.violation_condition: A shortened form first appears without the full words it represents being given.
when: Check the first use of a shortened form in the content.
rules.why: G-4 combines the two first-use expansion instructions; this remains separate from the rule deciding whether a shortened form should be used at all.

covers.quote: To help people understand specialist or technical content:

rules.quote: include a short summary without using specialist terms.
rules.specification: Look for a concise account of the content's main points in non-specialist language. The page does not set a numerical limit for ‘short’.
rules.violation_condition: Specialist or technical content lacks a short summary in non-specialist language, or its summary itself uses specialist terms.
when: Apply to specialist or technical content.
rules.why: The list lead-in supplies the condition; the summary is a distinct document component, not another instance of explaining an individual term.
